attachments.text:
ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-01-15
Provider: Dr. Sarah Chen, MD
Department: Pediatrics
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Persistent nighttime coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
He has a history of asthma diagnosed at age 6 and uses an albuterol inhaler as needed, which provides temporary relief. His parents note that during spring and fall, his symptoms become significantly worse, especially when he plays soccer outdoors. Despite no recent hospitalizations or emergency visits, he often wakes up coughing and feels tightness in his chest when running, even with prior use of albuterol. One week later, the child reports improved sleep and better exercise tolerance. He has used his rescue inhaler less frequently and feels more confident during physical activity.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Moderate persistent asthma
- Allergic rhinitis
- Atopic dermatitis
- Nasal polyps
- Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD)

He also has a history of allergic rhinitis and eczema.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- None

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Fluticasone propionate/salmeterol xinafoate (Advair HFA) 115/21 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily
- Albuterol sulfate (Ventolin HFA) 90 mcg, 2 inhalations every 4-6 hours as needed for wheezing or chest tightness
- Fluticasone propionate nasal spray 50 mcg per spray, 2 sprays each nostril once daily

ALLERGIES:
Tree and grass pollen (seasonal), Aspirin and NSAIDs (respiratory hypersensitivity), Dust mites

FAMILY HISTORY:
His younger sister has similar allergic tendencies

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: High school student (9th grade).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Physical examination reveals clear lungs at rest, but expiratory wheezes are heard after exertion.

PLAN:
The physician adds a new oral medication to his regimen to help with both asthma control and allergy-related inflammation.

attachments.text:
ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2021-01-15
Provider: Dr. James Okafor, MD
Department: Pulmonology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Follow-up for poor asthma control despite adherence to maintenance inhalers

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient returns for follow-up of his moderate persistent asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and nasal polyps, following initial evaluation one year ago for nighttime coughing and exercise-induced dyspnea. He reports poor control of his symptoms despite adherence to a regimen of fluticasone and salmeterol. He experiences wheezing and chest tightness several times per week and has had three asthma exacerbations in the past six months requiring oral corticosteroids. Over the next few weeks, the patient reports significant improvement in both asthma symptoms and nasal congestion.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Moderate persistent asthma (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Allergic rhinitis
- Atopic dermatitis
- Nasal polyps
- Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD)

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- None

MEDICATIONS:
He takes fluticasone and salmeterol.

Home Medications:
- Fluticasone propionate/salmeterol xinafoate (Advair HFA) 115/21 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily
- Albuterol sulfate (Ventolin HFA) 90 mcg, 2 inhalations every 4-6 hours as needed for wheezing or chest tightness
- Fluticasone propionate nasal spray 50 mcg per spray, 2 sprays each nostril once daily

ALLERGIES:
Tree and grass pollen (seasonal), Aspirin and NSAIDs (respiratory hypersensitivity), Dust mites

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Mother with asthma and seasonal allergies
- Father with eczema
- Maternal grandfather with nasal polyps

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: High school student (9th grade).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
His pulmonologist decides to add a medication that targets the inflammatory pathway upstream of leukotriene production to better control his symptoms.

He is advised to return for regular liver function monitoring while on this new medication.
